nutshell: Aerial-ground person ReID (matching people between drone and ground-camera views) lacks large, diverse video benchmarks. This paper introduces AG-VPReID, the largest such dataset to date (6,632 identities, 32,321 tracklets, 9.6M frames from drones up to 120m, CCTV, and wearable cameras), plus AG-VPReID-Net, a three-stream model that combines temporal-3D-shape modeling, physics-informed appearance normalization, and multi-scale attention to handle the extreme viewpoint, scale, and resolution gaps between aerial and ground footage.
contributions: AG-VPReID dataset: the largest video-based aerial-ground ReID benchmark to date (6,632 identities vs. the next-largest G2A-VReID's 2,788; 32,321 tracklets; 9.6M frames), the first to combine drone footage (up to 120m altitude, exceeding prior datasets' 60m max), CCTV, and first-person wearable cameras in one benchmark, with soft-biometric attribute annotations and some multi-day clothing-change tracking.

AG-VPReID-Net: a three-stream architecture - an Adapted Temporal-Spatial stream (CLIP features + GRU-based 3D SMPL shape regression + an identity memory bank) for motion-robust representations, a Normalized Appearance stream (PhysPT pose estimation + Texformer UV-texture maps, normalized and aggregated across frames) for resolution/appearance robustness, and a Multi-Scale Attention stream (frozen CLIP backbone + lightweight transformer decoder over multi-layer tokens) for scale robustness across drone altitudes - fused via a reciprocal-rank retrieval fusion step.

State-of-the-art results on AG-VPReID and four existing video ReID benchmarks (MARS, LS-VID, iLIDS-VID, G2A-VReID), plus a breakdown analysis isolating how much altitude versus clothing change each independently degrades matching accuracy.
deficiencies: The full 3-stream model barely outperforms Stream 1 alone in the main ablation (Table 5): St-1 alone reaches 71.52% A2G / 74.80% G2A Rank-1, while the full St-123 model reaches only 71.91% / 75.57% - a ~0.4-0.8 point gain despite adding two entire extra network streams that perform far worse individually (58.40% and 61.65% A2G alone), raising the question of whether streams 2 and 3's added architectural complexity is justified by their marginal contribution to the ensemble.

The paper never tests AG-VPReID-Net on any clothes-changing-specific ReID benchmark (e.g. CCVID, VCCR, MEVID, all cited and tabulated in Table 1) despite clothing change being one of the dataset's own headline features - the claimed 'generalizability across different settings' is only demonstrated on datasets without clothing changes or extreme viewpoint shifts.

Table 3 shows the Ground-to-Aerial test protocol includes 3,619 additional distractor identities not present in the Aerial-to-Ground direction, an asymmetry in test-set difficulty between the two reported directions that isn't discussed or controlled for when comparing A2G vs. G2A numbers.

Only 3,013 of the dataset's 6,632 total identities (those with both ground and aerial views) are actually used in the reported experiments, and the paper doesn't explain what distinguishes the excluded ~3,600 identities or why they were left out of the main protocol.

The dataset's privacy handling (Sec. 3.4) is limited to a brief mention of automated face-blurring, with no evaluation of how much this affects ReID-relevant appearance cues, and no discussion of how incidental third-party faces captured by the first-person wearable cameras (bystanders who aren't the tracked subject) were handled.
notable: The paper explicitly separates the effect of altitude/viewpoint changes from clothing changes (Table 7) and finds altitude change hurts far more - a 27.66% Rank-1 drop from 15m to 120m, versus only a 7.85% drop from clothing changes alone in ground-to-ground matching - a reusable empirical finding for prioritizing where aerial-ground ReID robustness work should focus, independent of this paper's specific method. Also worth noting: the Multi-Scale Attention stream keeps its CLIP backbone entirely frozen and trains only a lightweight transformer decoder on top, a parameter-efficient way to add scale robustness without fine-tuning a large vision backbone.
